he often avoided the <term>heretic</term> <gloss>one who holds dissenting religious opinions</gloss> because of his skill in debate. His lifestyle was not austere; rather, he used his wealth with great moderation. He delighted in white clothing and spent his time bathing twice a day in the public baths. Once, when someone asked him why, as a bishop, he bathed twice a day, he replied, "Because I do not have time for a third." Another time, seeing Arsatius the bishop, he was asked by one of Arsatius's circle why he wore clothing unsuitable for a bishop, and where it was written that a clergyman should dress in white. He replied, "First you tell me where it is written that a bishop must wear black clothing." When the questioner was at a loss, Sisinnius added to his counter-question: "You will not be able to show that a clergyman must wear black. But Solomon advised me, saying, 'Let your garments be white.' And the Savior in the Gospels appears wearing white clothing. Furthermore, he showed Moses and Elijah to the apostles wearing white." Having readily said these things and many others, he was greatly admired by those present.

When Leontius, the bishop of the Novatians in Ancyra in Galatia, was taking away a church and was visiting the city of Constantinople, Sisinnius came to him and urged him to return the church. Leontius replied heatedly, saying to him, "You Novatians do not deserve to have churches, as you reject repentance and shut out the philanthropy of God." When Leontius said these and many other such things against the Novatians, Sisinnius said, "And yet, no one repents as I do." When the father asked again, "How do you repent?" Sisinnius replied, "Because I saw you."

Once, when Bishop John was accusing him and saying that the city could not have two bishops, Sisinnius said, "It does not have two." When John became angry and said, "You see that you wish to be the only bishop," Sisinnius said, "I do not mean that, but rather that I am not a bishop in your eyes alone, though I am to others." John, indignant at what was said, replied, "But I will stop speaking with you, for you are a heretic." To this, Sisinnius wittily replied, "But I will provide the baths if you would relieve me of such great labor." Softened by this reply, John said, "I will not stop speaking with you if the mere act of speaking pains you so much."

Thus, Sisinnius was ready with his replies and witty. To write down and record all the things he said would be a long task. Therefore, I have shown what he was like in a few words, considering that sufficient. I will say this, however: he was famous for his learning. Because of this, all the bishops in succession loved and honored him. Furthermore, all the prominent members of the Senate loved and admired him. He wrote many books. In them, he hunts for words and mixes in poetic terms. He was admired more for his speaking than for his writing. For he possessed grace in his face, his voice, his posture, his gaze, and the entire movement of his body. He was therefore loved for these reasons by all religious groups, and especially by Bishop Atticus. These are the things concerning Sisinnius.

You shall sacrifice a pure maiden to the gods of the underworld,
Chosen by lot from the blood of the Aepytids,
In nocturnal slaughter.
And if she be slaughtered by another, then
You shall give others to be slaughtered willingly.
When the god had declared this, they immediately cast lots among all the maidens of the Aepytid lineage. The lot fell upon the daughter of Lyciscus. The seer Epebolus forbade this, saying it should not be done; for she was not the daughter of Lyciscus. He claimed that the woman who had lived with Lyciscus was unable to bear children, and that in this situation, the child had been passed off as his. While he was revealing these things regarding her, Lyciscus, taking the maiden with him, deserted to Sparta. When the Messenians were despondent upon realizing that Lyciscus had fled, Aristodemus, a man of the Aepytid lineage, more distinguished than the rest in reputation and in matters of war, offered his own daughter to be sacrificed willingly. But fate often conceals the eagerness of men, and the mud of the river, which even then hindered Aristodemus as he strove to save Messene, brought about an obstacle of this kind. A certain Messenian man (whose name they do not mention) happened to be in love with the daughter of Aristodemus. At that time, he was already intending to take her as his wife. This man initially entered into a dispute with Aristodemus, claiming that since he had betrothed her, Aristodemus was no longer the master of the girl, and that he himself, having betrothed her, had become more entitled than him. Secondly, when he saw that this was not succeeding for him, he turned to a shameless argument, claiming that he had had relations with the girl and that she was pregnant by him. Finally, he drove Aristodemus to such a point that, maddened by anger, he killed his daughter. Afterward, he cut her open and showed that she was not pregnant. Epebolus, who was present, ordered that someone else be provided to sacrifice the daughter; for the death of Aristodemus' daughter was of no use to them; the father had killed her, but they had not sacrificed her to the gods as the Pythia had commanded. When the seer said these things, the multitude of the Messenians rushed to kill the suitor of the girl, as he had brought an unnecessary stain upon Aristodemus and had made their hope of salvation uncertain. This man was a very close friend of Euphaes. Euphaes persuaded the Messenians that the oracle had been fulfilled by the death of the girl and that what had been done by Aristodemus was sufficient for them. When he said this, all those of the Aepytid lineage said he spoke the truth, for the fear regarding the daughter was removed from them, and each hastened; some, persuaded by the king's exhortation, dissolved the assembly and turned from it to sacrifices and the festival of the gods. The Lacedaemonians, having heard the oracle that had been given to the Messenians, were despondent, both they and their kings, and were hesitant to begin the battle in other respects as well. In the sixth year after the flight of Lyciscus from Ithome, the Lacedaemonians (for the omens were favorable to them) marched against Ithome. The Cretans did not happen to be present with them. The allies of the Messenians also arrived late. For the Spartans were already suspicious of other Peloponnesians, and especially of the Arcadians and Argives. The Argives were secretly intending to arrive, but more privately than by a common decree. For the Arcadians, the campaign had been forbidden openly. Yet even they did not arrive. For the reputation of the oracle had led the Messenians to risk the battle even without allies. In most respects, nothing different happened than in the previous battle, and the day left them fighting then as well. However, they do not record that either wing or company was forced back. For they say that the ranks did not remain as they were drawn up from the beginning, but that the best men from both sides came together in the very center, and there the entire struggle took place. Come, O heart, go to the sky, go to the pasture of God;

Place all your hope upon that which you have no hope for,

POLITICS
<note>The text begins with a discussion of the statesman's need for capable assistants, using the metaphor of a ship's captain and helmsman.</note> ...the captain and the shipowner. Just as they know well how to handle the rudder at the stern and how to tighten the yardarm when the wind rises, and just as an architect chooses assistants and craftsmen who will not ruin his work but will cooperate in the best possible way, so the statesman, being a master craftsman according to Pindar, and a creator of good order and justice, will not immediately choose friends who are merely like-minded, or servants who share his enthusiasm for the good, but rather those who are useful for different needs at different times, and who do not touch him unjustly or violently. For he will be seen as no different from a builder or carpenter who, through inexperience and error, uses corners and rules and lines that would cause the work to be distorted. For friends are the living and thinking instruments of statesmen, and one must not slide into error with them, but pay attention so that they do not commit wrongs without their knowledge. This is what shamed Solon and discredited him before the citizens. For when he took it upon himself to lighten the debts and introduce the <term>seisachtheia</term> <gloss>shaking off of burdens</gloss>, which was a euphemism for the cancellation of debts, he shared this with his friends, but they did a most unjust thing. They anticipated the law and borrowed a large amount of money, and shortly after the law was brought to light, they were seen to have purchased brilliant houses and much land with the money they had borrowed. Solon was accused of being a partner in the injustice. Agesilaus, regarding the ambitions of his friends, was himself very weak and humble, like the Pegasus of Euripides, yielding more than he wished, and by helping more readily in their misfortunes than was necessary, he seemed to be complicit in their injustices. For he saved Phoebidas after he was judged, for seizing the Cadmea without orders, claiming that such things should be done spontaneously, and he saved Sphodrias, who was brought to trial for a terrible and illegal act; for he had invaded Attica while they were allies, and he was released through the erotic pleas of his son, which softened the judge. A letter of his is carried, which says: "If Nicias has not done wrong, let him go; if he has done wrong, let him go for my sake; but in any case, let him go." But Phocion would not even enter the court for his son-in-law, who was on trial regarding the Harpalus affair, but said, "I made you my son-in-law for all that is just," and went away. And Timoleon the Corinthian, when he could not dissuade his brother from tyranny by teaching and begging him, acted against those who killed him; for one must not be a friend to the point of the altar, as Pericles once said, but to the point of every law and justice and common interest, which, if overlooked, leads to great and common harm, as the failure to punish Sphodrias and Phoebidas led to. For these men were not the least of the causes that plunged Sparta into the Leuctrian War. Since the statesman is not forced by reason to trample on friends for moderate mistakes, but rather to give them support, having placed the greatest public matters in a safe position, he may help his friends from his surplus and stand by them and work for them. There are also favors that are blameless and unenviable, such as helping a friend to obtain an office, or rather entrusting him with some honorable administration or a philanthropic embassy, such as one holding the honors of a leader or an appeal for friendship and harmony. But if there is some difficult task, and a great deed is prominent, he should assign him to this first, then choose him as a companion, as Diomedes did: "If you command me to choose a companion myself, how could I forget the godlike Odysseus?" And he in turn gives back the praise: "The horses, old man, which you ask about, are Thracian, whose master the good Diomedes killed, and twelve of his best companions beside him."

PRECEPTS
...yielding to friends no less adorns those who are praised than those who praise, but stubbornness, as Plato says, is a companion of solitude. Furthermore, in kind and philanthropic favors, one must make friends partners, and he urges them to praise and love those who have done well, as they have been both causes and advisors. But as for base and absurd demands, one should brush them off, not bitterly, but gently, teaching and comforting them, as they are not worthy of their virtue and reputation. Epaminondas did this best, when he refused Pelopidas's request to release a pimp from prison, but shortly after, when his mistress asked, he released him, saying, "Such favors, Pelopidas, are fitting for a mistress, not for a general." And Cato the Censor, when his friend, who was among his closest associates, asked for the release of one of those being judged by him, said, "It is shameful, you who ought to be correcting us young men, to be cast out by our own servants." For it was possible to refuse the favor in deed, but to remove the speed and bitterness from the words, so as not to inflict pain by the act itself, but necessarily because of the law and justice. There are also ways to help friends in politics regarding financial gain, such as Themistocles, who, after the battle, seeing a dead man wearing gold necklaces and bracelets, passed by, but turning to his friend, said, "Take these, for you are not Themistocles." For the situation often gives this to the statesman regarding his friends, for they are not all Menemachus; to one, entrust a paid advocacy for justice, to another, introduce a wealthy man needing care and patronage, to another, assist in some contract or lease that has profit. Epaminondas, when a wealthy man approached him, ordered him to ask for a talent, as if he himself had ordered him to give it. When the man came back and asked the reason, he said, "Because this man is a good man and is poor, while you are wealthy, having stolen much from the city." And Xenophon says that Agesilaus took pride in enriching his friends while he himself was superior to money.

Since, according to Simonides, every lark must have a crest, and politics brings some enmities and differences, it is not least appropriate for the statesman to be prepared for this. Many praise Themistocles and Aristides for laying aside their enmity at the borders whenever they went out on an embassy or a campaign, and then taking it up again. But to some, the case of Cretinas of Magnesia is wonderfully pleasing. For Hermias, who was in political opposition to a man who was ambitious and noble in soul, when the Mithridatic war seized the city and he saw it in danger, ordered Hermias to take over the government and manage the affairs, and if he wished to command, he himself would go out of the way, so that they would not, by competing with each other, destroy the city. The proposal pleased Hermias, and saying that Cretinas was more sensible than himself, he withdrew with his children and wife. And Cretinas sent him away, giving him of his own money what was most useful for those fleeing and besieged, and having managed the city in the best way, he saved it unexpectedly from being destroyed. For if it is noble and high-minded to proclaim, "I love my children, but I love my country more," it is surely no less ready for each to say, "I hate so-and-so, and I wish to do him harm, but I love my country more." For not wishing to be reconciled with an enemy, for whose sake one must sacrifice a friend, is terribly savage and beastly.

### The Fourth Chapter: On the Common Rules for Vomiting and Diarrhea, and an Indication of the Method of Drawing with Laxative and Emetic Medicines

It is said that whoever wishes to use a laxative, or vomit, or digest their food, should take the amount they intend to consume in a day in several portions, and make them different types of food and different types of drink. The stomach is affected by this variety, so it desires to expel what is inside it either upward or downward. As for food that is not varied, or food taken on top of other food, the stomach rejects it, becomes distressed, and grips it tightly, especially if the amount is small. As for milk, nature does not require any of that. Know that the need for vomiting, diarrhea, and the like does not occur in one who manages their health well; they need what is lighter than these. Sometimes, however, they are necessary for the sake of health, refinement, and cleansing.

If the body is full, and the fullness is of the best humors—meaning blood—then phlebotomy is what is needed for purification, rather than diarrhea. If necessity dictates phlebotomy or evacuation by means of a laxative or strong medicines, one must begin with phlebotomy. This is among the recommendations of Hippocrates in the Book of the Epidemics <note>original: "Kitab al-Amsab"</note>. This is when the humors are mixed with the ailment and the blood. But if the humors are viscous and cold, sometimes phlebotomy increases their thickness and viscosity, so it is necessary to begin with diarrhea. In general, if the humors are balanced, prioritize phlebotomy. If the body is overwhelmed by them, evacuate. If they are not balanced, evacuate the excess first until they are balanced, then perform phlebotomy. If one prioritizes medicine over phlebotomy, and it is appropriate to prioritize phlebotomy by a few days, or if the patient was recently bled and needs evacuation, the medicine is sufficient for him. Often, taking the necessary medicine while phlebotomy is required causes disturbance and agitation, for it does not settle with sedatives. Know that phlebotomy should have been prioritized. Evacuation is not needed only for excessive fullness; the nature of the ailment and the fullness according to quality, not quantity, often call for it. Often, improving one's regimen suffices instead of the phlebotomy required at the time. Often, the patient is called to evacuate, but an obstacle prevents it; in that case, there is nothing for it but fasting, sleep, and correcting the imbalance caused by the fullness. Some evacuation is by way of precaution, such as what is needed by those accustomed to gout, epilepsy, or other conditions at a known time, especially in the spring. It is necessary to take precautions before the time and perform the evacuation specific to the disease, whether it be phlebotomy or diarrhea. Sometimes the use of external enemas and drying medicines is a form of evacuation, as is done by those with dropsy. You may need to use a medicine that is similar in quality to the humor being evacuated, such as scammony when you need to evacuate bile. It is necessary to mix with it something that opposes it in quality but agrees with it in purgation, such as myrobalan, and to correct any imbalance that may occur afterward. In patients with swelling of the viscera, their diarrhea and vomiting are weakened. If you are forced to do so, use something like ivy or safflower. As for <term>turbith</term> <gloss>a purgative root</gloss>, colocynth, and the like, Hippocrates said: if the patient is young and nature is easily inclined to vomit, the best way to cleanse him is to use vomiting in summer, spring, or autumn, but not in winter. If he is of moderate heat, diarrhea is better for him. If he is called to evacuate by vomiting, he should not wait for summer, and he should be careful when there is no need. It is necessary to precede diarrhea and vomiting by thinning the humor one wishes to evacuate and by widening and opening the passages, for that protects the body from fatigue. Know that accustoming nature to respond easily to what is desired of diarrhea or vomiting before using strong medicine is one of the methods of preparation. Diarrhea and vomiting with emaciation of the abdomen are difficult, tiring, and dangerous. An emetic medicine may act as a laxative if the stomach is strong, or if it is taken on an empty stomach, or if the person taking it has a loose nature, or is not accustomed to vomiting, or if the medicine is of a substance that is quickly digested. A laxative may act as an emetic due to the weakness of the stomach, or the extreme dryness of the waste, or the nature of the medicine, or if the person taking it has a thick constitution. Every laxative medicine, if it does not purge or if it purges without being digested, stirs up the humor it is meant to purge and spreads it through the body, so it takes hold of the body and other humors are transformed into it, increasing that humor in the body. Some humors are more inclined to vomiting in most cases, such as bile. Some are resistant to vomiting, such as black bile. Some have one state and another, such as phlegm. Diarrhea is more correct in itself. Whoever has a humor that is descending, such as those with intestinal colic, for them, vomiting is impossible. The worst laxative medicines are those composed of medicines that differ greatly in the time of their action, so the diarrhea becomes disturbed, and the first purges the second before it purges the latter, and sometimes the first purges the second itself. Whoever is subjected to diarrhea and vomiting while his body is clean will have no choice but dizziness, fainting, and distress. What is evacuated is evacuated with great difficulty. In general, as long as the medicine is evacuating the superfluous, there is no disturbance with it. When it begins to disturb, it is either evacuating something other than the superfluous, or when the humor to be evacuated is finished, it continues to diarrhea or vomit another humor, so the body is not cleansed of the humor intended for evacuation. And so on.</meta>

If he leaves two sisters and a wife, and bequeaths to a man the equivalent of a sister's share minus one-eighth of what remains of the wealth after the bequest, the method for this is that you establish the estate at twelve shares. For each sister is one-third of what remains of the wealth after the bequest. This is wealth minus a bequest. You know that one-eighth of what remains plus the bequest equals the share of a sister. So, one-eighth of what remains is one-eighth of the wealth minus one-eighth of the bequest. Thus, one-eighth of the wealth minus one-eighth of the bequest plus the bequest equals the share of a sister. That is one-eighth of the wealth and seven-eighths of a bequest. The entire wealth equals three-eighths of the wealth and one-third of the bequests and five-eighths of a bequest. Subtract three-eighths from the wealth, and there remains five-eighths of the wealth, which equals three bequests and five-eighths of a bequest. It was previously held by his brother, Musa, but the Sultan al-Nasir <note>referring to the Mamluk Sultan of Egypt</note> removed him from it and compensated him with something else. He sent an emir and an army to the city, and subsequently, Sultan Badr al-Din took control of it, established his kingdom, and his rule there became stable. I met this sultan outside the city as he was returning from hunting. I dismounted from my mount for him, and he dismounted from his mount and I greeted him. He turned his attention toward me. It is the custom of the kings of these lands that when a visitor dismounts for them, they dismount for him. This action pleases them, and they increase his honor. If he greets them while remaining mounted, they dislike it and are not pleased, which becomes a cause for the visitor’s deprivation. This happened to me with some of them, and I learned from it. When I greeted him, he mounted and I mounted, and he asked about me and my companions. I entered the city with him, and he ordered that I be lodged in the best lodging. He used to send much food, fruit, and sweets in copper vessels, along with candles and clothing. We did not stay with him for long.

We departed for the city of Aqsaray (pronounced with a fatha on the hamza, a sukun on the qaf, a fatha on the undotted sad, and a ra). It is one of the most beautiful cities of Anatolia. It is surrounded by stone houses and gardens on every side. Three rivers flow through the city, and water runs through its houses, trees, and grapevines. Inside it are many gardens. They manufacture there the carpets attributed to it, made of sheep's wool, which have no equal in any other land. From there, they are exported to Syria, Egypt, Iraq, India, China, and the lands of the Turks. This city is under the obedience of the King of Iraq. Arafah is a village containing farms, vegetables, and melon fields. It has fine houses for the people of Mecca, who stay there on the day of Arafah. The place of standing <note>al-Mawqif</note> is near it, at a mountain called Ilal. There are water cisterns, basins, and a flowing canal there. A marker has been built, behind which the Imam stands for the prayer, with the people around him and on the mountains near it. The prayer ground <note>al-Musalla</note> is on the edge of the valley of Uranah, on the borders of Arafah. It is not permitted to stand within the valley. In the prayer ground, there is a pulpit made of brick, and behind it is a large basin. Two miles before it are the two mountain passes <note>al-Ma'zamayn</note>, which are the boundary of the Sacred Precinct <note>al-Haram</note>. The valley of Muhassir is a valley between Mina and Muzdalifah, and it is the boundary of Muzdalifah. Al-Tan'im is a place with mosques around the mosque of Aisha and water cisterns on the Medina road. From there, the Meccans enter the state of consecration <note>ihram</note> for the Lesser Pilgrimage <note>Umrah</note>. White markers surround the Sacred Precinct. From the west, al-Tan'im is three miles away; from the Iraq road, nine miles; from the Yemen road, seven miles; from the Ta'if road, eleven miles; and from the main road, ten miles.
